questions.explanation: Any non-zero number is truthy, so a value of 994 enters the first branch and 'yes' is logged. Only values such as zero and empty strings are falsy. The printed value is yes, while the alternatives come from treating any positive number as false, assuming the branch prints nothing and confusing the condition with a numeric result.
questions.hint: Remember which primitive values are falsy in a condition.

options.misconception: Assuming dividing a number by text yields a number
Confusing the test with the value tested

questions.explanation: Dividing 996 by a non-numeric string produces NaN, and Number.isNaN returns true for that value. The global isNaN would first coerce, which differs from the strict method. The printed value is true, while the alternatives come from assuming dividing a number by text yields a number, confusing the test with the value tested and thinking the conversion throws.
questions.hint: Number.isNaN does not coerce its argument.

options.misconception: Taking the radix as the result

questions.explanation: parseInt reads leading digits in base ten and returns the number 997. The radix argument selects the base; it is not part of the answer. Both the direct number 997 and the equivalent sum 498 plus 499 match, whereas 998 and 10 come from rounding the parsed value up and taking the radix as the result.
questions.hint: The second argument names the numeric base.

questions.explanation: for...in visits the enumerable keys a and b, so the concatenated string has length two. The numeric values, including 999, are never visited by this loop.
